description: We are an innovation-driven team of siblings participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal is to leverage data analysis, artificial intelligence, and technology to identify meaningful Earth system trends and develop impactful solutions. We value collaboration, creative problem-solving, and diverse perspectives. We welcome developers, data analysts, researchers, designers, and Earth science enthusiasts to join us in turning data into meaningful discoveries.
summary:
TrendLens turns anyone into an Earth system trend detective. NASA measures hundreds of variables, but students and the public hit three walls: which variables to look at, how to get a long, clean record for a place, and how to tell a real trend from noise. 

TrendLens follows the challenge's four steps: Ask, Find, Test, Explain. Pick a topic and a place, or type a question, and TrendLens ranks 12 NASA variables (MERRA-2 and CERES via NASA POWER, plus MODIS tree cover and NDVI) by how much they changed. It tests each one with an autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall test and a Theil-Sen slope, then explains the verdict in one plain sentence.

Each result comes with a grid-cell map, a NOAA weather-station cross-check, and an impact panel built from 25 published sources. Six featured regions cover 72 trends (42 significant, 33 opposite-direction pairs), and live mode analyses any spot or region on Earth in the browser. TrendLens says "not significant yet" when that is the honest answer, never claims causes, and links every result to Giovanni, AppEEARS and KNMI so users can check it themselves.
details:
TrendLens: Be an Earth system trend detective
Live app: https://cosmosis.earth

WHAT IT DOES 
NASA measures hundreds of things about our planet: temperature, rain, soil moisture, vegetation, haze, sunlight, clouds and wind. Students and the public hit three walls when they try to use this data:
1. With so many variables, which ones should they look at?
2. How do they get a long, clean record for the place they care about.
3. When a line goes up, how do they know it's a real trend and not just noise?

TrendLens removes all three. It follows the challenge's four steps:
1. Ask: choose a topic (Heat, Water & rain, Vegetation, Air & sunlight) and a place. Six featured regions are included: Central Sahel, India's Indo-Gangetic Plain, the North China Plain, the Southern Amazon, the US Southwest and the Canadian Prairies. You can also type a question in your own words, such as "Is it getting hazier over Delhi?", or click anywhere on a 3D globe.
2. Find: the Trend Radar tests all 12 variables for that place. It ranks them by signal-to-noise: how far each one moved over its record, compared with its normal year-to-year swings. Beginners can see what's worth a closer look without being experts.
3. Test: every trend gets a proper statistical test and a plain-language verdict, for example: "Air temperature in the Southern Amazon is rising by about 0.48 °C per decade (95% interval +0.31 to +0.64). This is unlikely to be chance (p < 0.001)."
4. Explain: a grid-cell map shows where the change is happening, weather stations check the satellite record, and an impact panel explains why the change matters for people.

HOW IT WORKS (DATA AND METHOD)
1) Data
- NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis (GMAO), 1981–2025, 45 years: air temperature, hottest-day temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, wind speed, root-zone soil wetness, and evaporation from land.
- NASA CERES SYN1deg (Langley), 2001–2025: sunlight reaching the ground, cloud cover, and aerosol optical depth (haze, smoke, dust).
- Both come through NASA POWER. It needs no login and lets a browser request data directly, which is what makes live analysis possible anywhere on Earth.
- MODIS Terra via ORNL DAAC:
- Tree cover (MOD44B), yearly.
- Vegetation greenness (NDVI, MOD13Q1), every 16 days at 250 m. We used 54 sample sites and 3,510 separate downloads.
- NOAA Climate Data Online (GSOM) weather stations: independent ground truth
- NASA GIBS imagery: behind every map and the 3D globe.

2) Processing pipeline (Python), applied to every variable
1. Download every grid cell in the region, every month, and keep only land cells so coastlines don't mix ocean into a land story.
2. Weight each cell by its true area, since cells shrink towards the poles. Skip missing values; never invent them.
3. Quality-check the record and reject anything shorter than 15 years. CERES variables start in 2001 on purpose, so two satellite products are never joined into a fake jump.
4. For NDVI, discard cloudy and invalid pixels, take the median of the good pixels at each site, keep the greenest image of each month, and use only sites with more than 80% of their record.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), data access for MERRA-2 and CERES
NASA POWER API (used for the featured regions and for live analysis in the browser)
MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA GMAO), with 7 variables from 1981–2025
CERES SYN1deg (NASA Langley), giving sunlight, cloud cover and aerosol optical depth from 2001–2025
MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 v061, vegetation greenness (NDVI)
MODIS Terra MOD44B v061, tree cover
ORNL DAAC MODIS Web Service (download of the MODIS subsets)
ORNL DAAC (Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): map tiles, MODIS true colour, borders and coastlines
NASA Blue Marble imagery (globe and map base layer via GIBS)
projectRefs: CSA RADARSAT Constellation Mission (cited on the Method page)
GEO.ca, Canada's geospatial data portal (linked from the Canadian Prairies page)
CSA open data and ecosystem monitoring resources
NOAA Climate Data Online, Global Summary of the Month (weather-station ground truth)
NOAA NCEI Access Data Service (live nearest-station requests)
KNMI Climate Explorer (linked from every result)
IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers
IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Summary for Policymakers
WHO: Climate change, heat and health
